title: Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab
hookLine: remembered with care for the sick at Bangla Sahib

lines: A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.
BOTTLES OF WATER FOR THE SICK.
cards: In the middle of New Delhi, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool. Day and night, people come with bottles to take its water home to someone sick. Its langar hall serves meals from morning to night.
And the whole place is built around the memory of a child, who came to Delhi because an emperor summoned him, and stayed to look after the sick. Today: Bangla Sahib.

teach.b: Guru Har Krishan was the younger son of Guru Har Rai. Before his father died, he named the boy as the eighth Guru; tradition says he was about five.
Some objected, including his older brother, Ram Rai, who had gone to the Mughal court and won favor there.
The emperor Aurangzeb summoned the young Guru to Delhi. There he stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh, a Rajput noble. That house is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib: bangla means bungalow.
While he was there, an epidemic struck the city; tradition usually names smallpox, and some accounts say cholera.
Tradition says the child Guru went out among the sick, of every faith, giving water and comfort and care. He caught the disease himself and died, still a child; tradition says he was about eight.
Asked who would follow him, tradition says, his last words were Baba Bakale: the next Guru is at Bakala, which proved to be Guru Tegh Bahadur.
The Sikh Ardas, which you learned line by line this year, remembers him in a single line. In paraphrase: remember Guru Har Krishan, at the sight of whom all suffering departs.
Today, the pool at Bangla Sahib is where people take water for the sick, in his memory. His gurpurab is marked there with kirtan and langar, and some Sikhs visit or serve the sick that day.
A very short life, remembered for care that walked toward the sickness instead of away from it.

how: On Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab, Sikhs gather at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and elsewhere for kirtan and langar; many take water from Bangla Sahib's pool to the sick and serve the unwell in his memory.

games.q: an epidemic sweeps Delhi while you, a child Guru, are staying in the city. what does tradition say you do?
o: go among the sick of every faith with water and care.
wait for the emperor's permission to act.
games.why: he cared for the sick, caught the illness himself, and died; Bangla Sahib stands where he stayed.

practice: Bring to mind one person you know who's sick, recovering or worn out, and picture them clearly. Hold them with care, and let one small, real kindness for them come to mind: a message, a meal, a ride, an hour of company.
If you pray, you can say the Ardas line for them in your own way, or just Waheguru.
